HOW TO VOTE
Rules and deadlines are different in every state. Always check the official sites:
Register to vote · vote.gov› How to vote, step by step · USA.gov› Find your polling place · USA.gov› Your state's election office · EAC›
WHERE TO VOTE

Find where to vote near you

Put in your zip code and we'll show you polling places on a map near you.

Your zip code only finds places near you. Your exact polling place depends on your home address — the official finder will ask for it.

Vote by mail — yes, you can

You can vote by mail in every state. Ask your state's election office for a mail ballot, fill it out at home, and send it back by mail or drop it in an official drop box before the deadline. Deadlines are different in every state, so request it early. In many states you can track your ballot online to make sure it was received and counted.

Vote by mail, step by step · USA.gov›Register to vote · vote.gov›

Voting laws — the basics

To vote in a federal election you must be a U.S. citizen, 18 or older on Election Day, and registered to vote where you live. Beyond that, the rules are different in every state: some states ask for a photo ID at the polls and some don't, registration deadlines are different, and early voting days are different. Always check your own state's official election office — never trust a random post about the rules.

Your state's election office · EAC›How to vote, step by step · USA.gov›
MAKE YOUR VOTE COUNT

Why your vote matters

Your vote picks the president, Congress, governors, and local leaders — and those leaders decide the taxes you pay, the border, energy, health care, schools, and whether America goes to war or makes peace. One vote can decide a close race, and close races decide the laws the whole country has to live under. Voting is how regular people shape the future, in America and in the world. Make your vote count.

WHAT THEY WANT · NEXT 4 YEARS

Republicans, Democrats & Trump

Tap a tab to see what each one is about — in plain words

Based on the Republican Party's 2024 national platform. Not every Republican agrees on every point.

AI imageREPUBLICANS

What Republicans are about

America First. A strong military, secure borders, American energy and manufacturing, lower taxes and fewer rules, and allies paying their share for defense. Republicans say the federal government should do less, and states, families and businesses should decide more.

AI image

In the world

Lead from strength. End the war in Ukraine quickly and restore peace in Europe and the Middle East. Build a missile defense shield over the whole country. Make America the dominant energy producer in the world — oil, gas, coal and nuclear.

AI image

China and trade

Put tariffs on Chinese goods, end China's most-favored-nation trade status, and bring manufacturing home. Use broad tariffs on imports to protect American jobs and help pay for tax cuts.

AI image

Immigration

Seal the border, finish the wall, and carry out large deportations of people here illegally.

At home

Big tax cuts, fewer rules, and no tax on tips. Protect Medicare and Social Security with no cuts. Protect the right to keep and bear arms. School choice, with education decisions returned to the states.

What's next — in the next 4 years

Finish the border wall. Keep tax cuts in place. Expand American energy. Strengthen the military. Keep the U.S. dollar as the world's reserve currency.

Based on the Democratic Party's 2024 national platform. Not every Democrat agrees on every point.

DEMOCRATS

What Democrats want in the world

Lead through alliances and diplomacy. Keep NATO strong, stand with Ukraine, work with other countries on climate and trade, and lower costs for working families at home.

In the world

Keep NATO strong and support allies. Keep military and economic aid to Ukraine, and stand with NATO against Russia. Support Israel's security, and push for diplomacy and a lasting peace in the Middle East.

China and trade

Use targeted tariffs on Chinese steel, chips and electric cars, and compete while keeping trade open in other areas. Oppose broad tariffs, saying they raise prices for families.

Climate and energy

Invest in clean energy at home, cut emissions, and work with other countries on climate. Build solar, wind and batteries in America.

Immigration

Secure the border and fix the system, with a path to citizenship for long-term residents like Dreamers.

At home

No tax rise for people earning under $400,000 a year. Billionaires and big companies pay more. Raise the minimum wage to at least $15 an hour. Protect and expand the Affordable Care Act, and lower prescription drug prices. Universal background checks for guns, and a ban on assault weapons. Invest in public schools.

What's next — in the next 4 years

Lower costs for families, expand health coverage, restore the abortion protections of Roe v. Wade, invest in clean energy, and keep alliances like NATO strong.

What Republicans say — why a liberal system can't work

Republicans say a bigger government costs regular people more. Higher taxes and more rules make it harder for small businesses to hire and grow. Energy rules that cut oil and gas push up gas and electric bills. More government spending adds to the national debt, which means higher prices and higher interest rates.

On the border, they say a softer system means more people coming in illegally, which puts pressure on hospitals, schools, and jobs. And when the federal government gets bigger, families and states get less say over their own lives.

How it could affect 2028

2028 will likely come down to what people feel every day — can they afford groceries, rent, and gas, do they feel safe, and is the border secure. If Democrats win in 2028 on a liberal platform, Republicans say you'd see more of it: higher taxes, more spending, stricter energy and business rules, and a softer border.

If voters reject it, that's the opening for Republicans — run on lower taxes, cheaper energy, a secure border, and less government.

Donald Trump is the 47th President. This is what his administration did in his second term, starting in January 2025, and what it says is next.

STILL IN CHARGE

Even if the Democrats won, President Trump is still in charge

The midterms change Congress, not the President. President Trump is President until January 20, 2029. The rules and laws he signed for our safety — like the Laken Riley Act — are still the law, and he runs the agencies that protect our border and keep Americans safe. He will always look after us and the American people.

DONALD TRUMP

What Trump did for our country

On his first day back, he declared a national emergency at the southern border, sent the military to help secure it, and started reversing many of the last administration's policies.

The border

Illegal border crossings fell sharply. He ended catch-and-release, expanded deportations, signed the Laken Riley Act, and named Mexican drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

Economy and taxes

In July 2025 he signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law, extending tax cuts and adding new tax relief, including no tax on tips. He put tariffs on imports from many countries, and the Treasury took in tens of billions of dollars in tariff duties. He also cut federal rules, which the administration says saved families money.

Energy

He declared an energy emergency, expanded oil and gas drilling permits, pulled the U.S. out of the Paris climate agreement again, and ended electric vehicle mandates.

In the world

NATO allies agreed to raise defense spending to 5% of GDP. The U.S. struck Iran's nuclear program. He made a minerals deal with Ukraine, and pushed for an end to the war there. Some of his orders were challenged in court, including the order on birthright citizenship.

What's next

Finish the border wall. Keep the tax cuts. Make America the dominant energy producer. Build a missile defense shield over the country. Prevent a world war and restore peace in Europe and the Middle East. Protect Social Security and Medicare with no cuts.

Sources: 2024 Republican and Democratic national platforms; White House and Congress records, 2025.

Fact Check

See the real record, with sources

CHECKING THE RECORD

In the real app, this shows what official records say, with links.

RECENT CHECKS
TRUE

The Laken Riley Act was the first bill President Trump signed in his second term.

Yes — signed Jan 29, 2025. It passed with both parties: 64-35 in the Senate, 263-156 in the House.White House — signing · NPR — first bill
TRUE

The 2025 government shutdown was the longest in US history.

Yes — Oct 1 to Nov 12, 2025, 43 days. The old record was 35 days in 2018-19.Wikipedia — 2025 shutdown · Brookings — shutdowns
TRUE

The One Big Beautiful Bill adds $3.4 trillion to the deficit.

The nonpartisan CBO says the law as signed adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over 10 years — over $4 trillion counting the interest.Bipartisan Policy Center — cost · Senate Budget Committee — CBO tally
MISLEADING

Health care subsidies ended, so nobody can get help paying for insurance anymore.

The extra subsidies did expire Dec 31, 2025 — but the regular ACA tax credits are still there, and the House passed a 3-year extension in January 2026. It is stuck in the Senate.GovTrack — House vote 230-196 · LegalClarity — what happened next

THE PEOPLE WITH THE POWER

The Elites

The people and groups with the most power over the world — and what they actually do with it

These are the people and groups at the top — the ones with the money, the meetings, and the power to shape what happens in the world. Every card below is a real person or group, with real numbers. No rumors — just what they actually do.

AI imageTHE MEETINGS

World Economic Forum

The club in Davos, Switzerland. Founded in 1971 by Klaus Schwab, it brings the world’s politicians, CEOs, and billionaires together every January to set the agenda. Schwab ran it for 55 years and stepped down in April 2025. Now the boss is BlackRock’s Larry Fink, who took over as interim co-chair in August 2025. Their big idea is ‘stakeholder capitalism’ — big business and big government working together.

Source: World Economic Forum, Aug 2025
AI imageTHE MONEY

BlackRock — Larry Fink

The biggest money manager on Earth. BlackRock handles about $15.5 trillion — around half the size of the whole U.S. economy. Its iShares funds alone hold over $6 trillion. One honest note: that money is not BlackRock’s own — it is the savings of pension funds, governments, and everyday investors, which BlackRock manages for a fee.

Source: BlackRock Q3 2026 earnings, Oct 2026
THE MONEY

George Soros

The billionaire funder. Soros made his fortune in the financial markets and has given away more than $32 billion to his Open Society Foundations, which fund progressive and liberal causes in countries all over the world — including in the United States.

Source: Open Society Foundations
THE MONEY

Bill Gates

The Microsoft co-founder — one of the richest men alive. His Gates Foundation is the biggest private foundation in the world: a $9 billion budget for 2026, mostly for global health and vaccines. Gates says he will spend $200 billion over the next 20 years and then close the foundation in 2045. Now hear his own words. In a 2010 TED talk he said: “The world today has 6.8 billion people. That’s headed up to about 9 billion. Now, if we do a really great job on new vaccines, health care, reproductive health services, we could lower that by, perhaps, 10 or 15 percent.” He says he means that when children survive, families choose to have fewer of them, so growth slows down. But a billionaire talking about cutting the population by 10 to 15 percent is exactly why a lot of people don’t trust him with that kind of power. Who gave him the right to decide how many of us there should be?

Source: TED talk, 2010 · Gates Foundation, Jan 2026
THE GLOBAL BODIES

World Health Organization

The world’s health boss, run by Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. In May 2025 its member countries adopted the first-ever Pandemic Agreement — a global plan for the next pandemic. It only takes effect once 60 countries ratify it. The United States left the WHO on January 22, 2026, under President Trump.

Source: WHO, May 2025; HHS, Jan 2026
AI imageTHE MEETINGS

Bilderberg Meeting

The private meeting. Every year since 1954, about 130 of the most powerful people in politics, business, and media meet behind closed doors — no cameras, no public record of what is said. The 72nd meeting was April 9–12, 2026, in Washington, D.C., with 128 leaders from 23 countries.

Source: Bilderberg Meetings, 2026
AI imageTHE GLOBAL BODIES

United Nations

The world’s biggest club of countries — 193 member nations, founded in 1945 after World War II. Its Secretary-General is António Guterres — until December 31, 2026. A new Secretary-General takes over on January 1, 2027. Its Security Council has 5 permanent members — the U.S., Britain, France, Russia, and China — and any one of them can veto a decision.

Source: United Nations
THE SCHOOLS OUR KIDS DESERVE

Schools & Fraud

The school system — and the fraud going on inside it

Schools are supposed to teach our kids. But behind the classrooms, real money has been stolen, test scores have been faked, and rich parents have bought their kids’ way in. Every card below is a real case, with real numbers. No rumors — just what actually happened.

AI imageTEST FRAUD

Atlanta Test Cheating

In Atlanta, teachers and principals changed students’ test answers to fake higher scores — because No Child Left Behind tied jobs and funding to test scores. A state investigation found 44 of 56 schools cheated on the 2009 state test, and 178 educators were implicated. 35 were indicted. In 2015, 11 of the 12 who went to trial were convicted of racketeering. The pressure to hit the numbers was so strong that cheating became the system.

Source: Georgia Bureau of Investigation, 2011; court verdict, Apr 1, 2015
AI imageCHARTER FRAUD

A3 Charter Schools — California

Sean McManus and Jason Schrock ran 19 online charter schools in California. Prosecutors say they faked enrollments — buying children’ personal information and signing up kids from summer sports programs who never took a class — and stole at least $400 million in state school money from 2016 to 2019. About $80 million of it was diverted. Both men pleaded guilty and agreed to give back more than $210 million, 13 houses, and company shares.

Source: San Diego County District Attorney
AI imagePHANTOM STUDENTS

ECOT — Ohio

The Electronic Classroom of Tomorrow was Ohio’s biggest online charter school. The state paid it about $1 billion over 20 years. Then auditors found it could not prove its students were actually doing the schoolwork it billed for — kids who only logged in, or never showed up at all. The state ordered more than $117 million repaid. ECOT shut down in January 2018 instead of paying it back.

Source: Ohio Auditor of State
ARIZONA

Santa Cruz County — Arizona

Right here in Arizona: Elizabeth Gutfahr, the elected treasurer of Santa Cruz County, wired about $38.7 million of public money — meant for schools, fire districts, and county services — into her own business accounts over 10 years. Nobody caught it for a decade. She pleaded guilty in November 2024 and was sentenced to 10 years in prison in June 2025, and ordered to pay back about $51.8 million. Arizona’s own Auditor General has documented fraud in 21 school districts — nearly $26 million misused.

Source: Arizona Auditor General Report 24-402; U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of Arizona
AI imageCOLLEGE BRIBES

Varsity Blues — College Admissions

Rich parents bought their kids’ way into top colleges. From 2011 to 2018, 33 parents paid more than $25 million to a man named Rick Singer, who faked SAT and ACT scores and bribed coaches to pretend their kids were star athletes. More than 50 people were charged in all, including actresses Felicity Huffman and Lori Loughlin. Singer was sentenced to three and a half years in prison in 2023. Regular families’ kids lost those spots.

Source: U.S. Department of Justice, Mar 2019

THE 2024 ELECTION

Why Most People Voted Republican Over Democrats

What the exit polls and post-election surveys say decided it

Donald Trump won 77.3 million votes — 49.8% to 48.3% — and swept all seven battleground states. It was close. But the exit polls and post-election surveys are clear about what tipped it. Real numbers, real sources — just what the voters themselves said.

AI imageTHE RESULT

Trump won 77.3 million votes — and swept all seven battleground states

Donald Trump beat Kamala Harris 77,303,568 votes to 75,019,230 — 49.8% to 48.3%. The Electoral College was 312 to 226, and he carried all seven battleground states: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. He was the first Republican to win the popular vote since George W. Bush in 2004. About 155 million people voted.

Source: American Presidency Project · Federal Election Commission
THE ECONOMY

Prices were the number one issue

75% of voters said inflation had caused them moderate or severe hardship in the past year, and 45% said they were worse off than four years earlier. Among Trump voters, 51% said the economy was the issue that mattered most. Voters trusted Trump over Harris to handle the economy by 54% to 45%. In the Navigator post-election survey, Trump led by 12 points on the economy and 13 points on inflation.

Source: CBS News exit poll · NBC News exit poll · Gallup · Navigator Research
THE BORDER

The border was the second-biggest reason

53% of Trump voters said he “will secure the border and fight illegal immigration” was one of their biggest reasons to vote for him. Immigration was the second-most important issue for Trump voters — 21% said it mattered most. 56% of Trump voters named protecting the borders one of the two most important issues in the election.

Source: Navigator Research · NBC News exit poll · Chamber of Progress
THE MOOD

Most voters thought the country was on the wrong track

About two-thirds of voters said the U.S. economy was in poor shape. 46% said their family's financial situation was worse than four years ago — more than double the 20% who said that in 2020. The election was a verdict on the last four years as much as a choice between two candidates.

Source: Edison Research exit poll
WHO MOVED

Hispanic voters, young men, and the working class moved to Trump

Hispanic voters went 46% for Trump, up from 32% in 2020 — the best for a Republican in exit polls going back to the 1970s. Young men went 49% for Trump, up from 41%. Voters earning under $50,000 a year flipped to Trump at 50%, and those earning $50,000 to $100,000 at 52%. Among Teamsters rank-and-file members, 59.6% backed endorsing Trump.

Source: Edison Research exit poll · Pew Research Center · RealClearPolling
THE OTHER SIDE

What Harris voters said mattered most — and why it did not carry the day

56% of Harris voters said democracy was the issue that mattered most to them, and 40% said standing against a national abortion ban was one of their top reasons. Those issues carried her base — but for the majority of voters, prices and the border weighed more.

Source: NBC News exit poll · Navigator Research
WHAT TO WATCH

What's Ahead?

What is coming up — and what to look out for

The next few months have a lot coming. Here is what is on the calendar, what it means, and what to watch for.

AI image
DEC 4, 2026

November jobs report — does hiring hold up?

The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the November jobs numbers on December 4. October was strong — 165,000 jobs added, unemployment 4.1%. Watch whether hiring holds up, or whether the layoffs at Amazon, UPS, and Oracle start showing up in the numbers.

Source: Bureau of Labor Statistics
DEC 8–9, 2026

The Fed meets — another rate hike?

The Federal Reserve meets December 8–9. Markets put about a 9-in-10 chance on another quarter-point hike, to 4.00–4.25%. Watch the size of the move — and what it means for mortgages, already at 7.28%, and for credit cards.

Source: CME FedWatch, Freddie Mac
DEC 17–20, 2026

AmericaFest in Phoenix

Turning Point USA's AmericaFest comes to the Phoenix Convention Center, December 17–20. Speakers include Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Erika Kirk, Karoline Leavitt, Tulsi Gabbard, Steve Bannon, and Matt Gaetz. It is the biggest conservative gathering of the year — and it is right here in Arizona.

Source: Turning Point USA
BEFORE DEC 31, 2026

A new boss for the United Nations

António Guterres's term as UN Secretary-General ends December 31, 2026, and his successor has not been chosen yet. Eight candidates are in the running. Watch who gets picked — the new chief takes over on January 1, 2027.

Source: United Nations, Reuters
JAN 3, 2027

A new Congress is sworn in

Democrats take control of both chambers on January 3, 2027, after winning the November 3 midterms. Watch what they do first — and whether the permitting bill the Senate just passed 62–33 ever gets a vote in the House before then.

Source: U.S. Senate, U.S. House
WINTER 2026–27

Heating bills: gas down, oil way up

The government's winter forecast: homes heating with natural gas should spend $640, down 9% from last winter. Homes heating with electricity pay $1,196, up 4%. Homes heating with oil face $2,115, up 21% — the steepest jump of all.

Source: U.S. Energy Information Administration
EARLY 2028

The 2028 race begins

Republican primaries begin in early 2028, the Republican National Convention meets in Houston in the summer, and Election Day is November 7, 2028. Watch who jumps in first — the field is already forming on the 2028 page.

Source: Red American News · 2028 Race
